full_judgment: 55. One of the cardinal principles of Criminal Justice which has always to be kept in view in our system of Administration of Criminal Justice for criminal cases is that a person arraigned as an accused is presumed to be innocent unless that presumption is rebutted by prosecution on production of evidence as may show him to be guilty of the offence with which he is charged and benefit of every reasonable doubt should be given to the accused and this doubt must be a supportable doubt and not a fanciful doubt. It is, also, to be kept in view that danger of exaggerated devotion to rule of benefit of doubt at the expense of social defence and to soothing sentiment that all acquittals are always good regardless of justice to victim and community, demand especial emphasis in contemporary context of escalating crime.
